sub: Named after al-qiyāmah, the Resurrection, which is also its whole subject
theme: The Resurrection is certain. The surah answers those who deny it: Allah will rebuild every bone, each person will face what he did, and people deny it only because they love this fleeting world.
story: Revealed in Makkah, very early. No report fixes the time, but the surah itself hints at it: midway, the Prophet ﷺ is told not to rush his tongue while receiving revelation, which happened while revelation was still new to him.

It answers people who denied the resurrection. One of them, reportedly ʿAdī ibn Rabīʿah, asked the Prophet ﷺ when and how the Day would come, then said: even if I saw it, I would not believe. Will Allah really gather bones?

The surah replies point by point: Allah can rebuild even the fingertips, no one escapes his record, and the real reason for denial is love of this world. It ends by asking: can the One who made you from a drop not raise the dead?

sections.title: By Resurrection Day: Allah can rebuild man’s bones, even his fingertips
sections.meaning: Allah swears by the Day of Resurrection and by the soul that blames itself. Does man think his bones won’t be gathered? Yes, Allah can rebuild even his fingertips. The real problem is that man wants to keep sinning, so he mockingly asks, “When is this Day?”
points: By the Day of Resurrection and the self-blaming soul
Gather his bones? Yes, even his fingertips
He wants to sin on, asking “When is that Day?”
sections.matters: The opening sets the surah’s case. The doubt is about bones; the answer goes even smaller, to the fingertips. And it exposes the real motive: denial comes from wanting to sin freely, not from a lack of proof.
sections.story: Reportedly revealed about ʿAdī ibn Rabīʿah, who asked the Prophet ﷺ when and how the Day would come, then said: “Even if I saw it, I would not believe. Will Allah gather bones?” Another report names Abū Jahl, who denied the resurrection.
explained: Lā uqsimu opens a strong oath; the lā adds force against the deniers’ claim. Allah swears by the Day of Resurrection itself, and by an-nafs al-lawwāmah, the soul that blames itself for wrongs, and even for not doing more good. The unstated answer: you will surely be raised.

Does man think Allah won’t gather his scattered bones? Balā: He can shape even his banān, the fingertips, the smallest and finest parts. Man’s problem isn’t proof. He wants to carry on sinning, or to deny what lies ahead, so he asks, “When is the Day of Resurrection?”, only to mock.
teaches: A conscience that blames itself is a sign of living faith.
The One who made you can remake you, down to your fingertips.
Denial often hides a wish to keep sinning.
Asking “when?” to mock changes nothing; the Day still comes.
sections.hook: Every ayah here ends in -ah: qiyāmah, lawwāmah, ʿiẓāmah, banānah, amāmah, qiyāmah. Yawm al-qiyāmah closes both ayah 1 and ayah 6.

sections.title: When the moon darkens, man finds no escape and witnesses against himself
sections.meaning: When eyes are dazzled, the moon goes dark and the sun and moon are brought together, man will cry, “Where is the escape?” No refuge; the only place to settle is with your Lord. He will be told all he sent ahead and left behind. He is his own witness, whatever excuses he offers.
points: Eyes dazzled, moon eclipsed, sun and moon brought together
“Where to flee?” No refuge; the return is to your Lord
Told of all he sent ahead and left behind
A witness against himself, despite his excuses
sections.matters: It answers “When is the Day?” by showing what that Day is like. Then it closes every exit: nowhere to run, no deed left out, and no excuse that works, because each person already knows what he did.
sections.story: No specific incident. It answers the mocking question in ayah 6.
explained: The mocker asked when. The answer: when baraqa al-baṣar, eyes are dazzled and stare in terror, the moon loses its light, and the sun and moon are brought together. Then man cries, ayna al-mafarr, where can I run? Kallā, lā wazar: no shelter, no mountain to hide on. Everyone’s final stop is with your Lord.

There he is told what he qaddama wa akhkhara: every deed, first and last, including practices he left behind that others followed. He hardly needs telling. Baṣīrah: he is his own witness, and his limbs testify against him, even if he throws out every excuse he has.
teaches: There is nowhere to run from Allah, only to Him.
What you start that others follow keeps counting after you.
You know yourself better than any excuse you make.
Your own limbs will speak about what you did.
sections.hook: The rhyme switches to -ar: baṣar, qamar, qamar, mafarr, wazar, mustaqarr, akhkhar. Yawmaʾidhin, “on that Day”, comes three times (10, 12, 13). Ayat 14–15 end in -rah.

sections.title: Don’t rush the revelation; on that Day faces are radiant or grim
sections.meaning: Midway, the Prophet ﷺ is told not to hurry his tongue with the revelation: Allah will gather it in his heart, have him recite it, and explain it. The deniers love the quick world and leave the Hereafter. That Day some faces will glow, looking at their Lord; others will be grim.
points: Don’t rush your tongue; gathering and reciting it is on Us
When We recite it, follow; explaining it is on Us too
No! You love the quick world and leave the Hereafter
Radiant faces, looking at their Lord
Grim faces, expecting a back-breaking blow
sections.matters: Allah guarantees the Prophet ﷺ both the words and the meaning of the Qurʾan. Then the surah names the root of denial, love of the here and now, and shows where each choice ends: faces that see their Lord, or faces that dread what is coming.
sections.story: The Prophet ﷺ found receiving revelation hard and would move his lips quickly, repeating after Jibrīl so as not to forget. Ayat 16–19 were revealed. After that he listened while Jibrīl recited, and recited it himself once Jibrīl left.
explained: While Jibrīl recited, the Prophet ﷺ would repeat along, afraid of losing a word. Allah tells him: don’t move your tongue to hurry it. Jamʿahu wa qurʾānahu: gathering it in your heart and making you recite it are on Us. When Jibrīl recites, listen, then follow. Bayānahu: explaining it is on Us too.

Kallā: the deniers love al-ʿājilah, the world that comes quickly, and leave the Hereafter. So see where it ends. Some faces will be nāḍirah, fresh and radiant, looking at their Lord. Others will be bāsirah, dark and scowling, sure that a fāqirah, a back-breaking calamity, is about to strike.
teaches: Allah protects the Qurʾan, its words and its meaning.
Listen fully before you repeat or reply.
Love of the quick world is what makes people neglect the Hereafter.
The greatest reward is to see Allah.
sections.hook: One root, ʿ-j-l, links both halves: li-taʿjala bih, “to hurry it” (16), and al-ʿājilah, “the quick world” (20). Wujūhun yawmaʾidhin comes at 22 and 24. Page 578 begins at ayah 20.

sections.title: The dying soul reaches the collarbones, then is driven to its Lord
sections.meaning: No! When the soul reaches the collarbones and people ask, “Who can cure him?”, the dying man is sure it is the parting. Shin is wrapped against shin, and on that Day the drive is to your Lord.
points: Soul at the collarbones; “Who can cure him?”
He knows it is the parting
Shin wrapped against shin
To your Lord, that Day, is the drive
sections.matters: From the Day of Resurrection the surah turns to something everyone sees: death. No doctor or healer can help, and at that moment it is too late to repent, so the time to turn back is before it comes.
sections.story: No specific incident. It reminds people of death, which no one can deny.
explained: Kallā: when the soul rises to at-tarāqī, the collarbones at the base of the throat, those around him ask, man rāq: who can heal him, or recite over him for a cure? Or it is the angels asking who will take his soul up. He is certain now: this is al-firāq, the parting from this world.

Wal-taffat as-sāqu bis-sāq: his lifeless shins are wrapped together, or the last day of this world meets the first of the next, hardship upon hardship. Then comes al-masāq: the soul is driven to its Lord, to be repaid for its deeds.
teaches: When death comes, no doctor or cure can hold the soul back.
Repent before the soul reaches the throat; then it is too late.
Death is the last day of this world and the first of the next.
Every soul is driven back to its Lord.
sections.hook: Ayah 30 echoes ayah 12: ilā rabbika yawmaʾidhin al-mustaqarr (12), ilā rabbika yawmaʾidhin al-masāq (30). Sāq (29) flows into masāq (30). This ends the first ruku.

sections.title: The strutting denier isn’t left aimless; his Maker can raise the dead
sections.meaning: He neither believed nor prayed; he denied, turned away and strutted home. Woe to you, then woe, again and again. Does man think he will be left aimless? He was a drop, then a clot, then shaped and made male or female. Is the One who did that unable to raise the dead?
points: Didn’t believe or pray; denied, turned away, strutted home
Woe to you, then woe; again woe, then woe
Does man think he’ll be left aimless?
A drop, a clot, shaped, made male and female
Can’t He give life to the dead?
sections.matters: It closes the surah’s argument. The denier’s life shows what denial produces: no faith, no prayer, only pride. Then the final proof: the One who made you from a weak drop can easily make you again.
sections.story: Reportedly about Abū Jahl. The Prophet ﷺ seized his clothes and said, “Awlā laka fa-awlā.” Abū Jahl replied, “Are you threatening me? Neither you nor your Lord can do anything to me.” Reports differ on whether ayah 34 came before or after this.
explained: Fa-lā ṣaddaqa wa lā ṣallā: no faith in his heart, no prayer in his actions. He denied and turned away, then went home to his family yatamaṭṭā, strutting and pleased with himself, without a care. Awlā laka fa-awlā: woe to you, and woe again, threat after threat, mocking the swagger of one who denies his Creator.

Does man think he will be left sudā: aimless, with no commands and no raising up? He began as a drop of fluid, then a clinging clot. Allah shaped and proportioned him, and made from him both sexes, male and female. The One who made all that from a weak drop can surely give life to the dead.
teaches: Faith in the heart shows in prayer; the denier has neither.
You were not created to be left without purpose.
Your own beginning is proof of your return.
When you recite ayah 40, answer: “Balā”, yes indeed.
sections.hook: A-yaḥsabu al-insān, “does man think”, appears twice: ayah 3 and ayah 36. The surah ends on a question (40) whose answer, balā, already came in ayah 4. The four woes form two pairs.

groups.text: Allah swears by the Day of Resurrection and by the soul that blames itself.
Does man think his bones won’t be gathered? Yes, Allah can rebuild even his fingertips.
Yet man wants to carry on sinning, and mockingly asks when the Day of Resurrection will be.
On that Day eyes are dazzled, the moon goes dark, and the sun and moon are brought together.
Man cries, “Where can I escape?” There is no refuge; the final stop is with your Lord.
Man is told all he did and left behind; he is his own witness, whatever his excuses.
Don’t hurry your tongue with the revelation: Allah will gather it in your heart, have you recite it, and explain it.
No! You love this quick world and neglect the Hereafter.
Some faces that Day will be radiant, looking at their Lord.
Other faces will be grim, sure that a back-breaking disaster is coming.
When the soul reaches the collarbones and people ask who can cure him, he knows it is the parting.
Shin wraps against shin, and that Day the drive is to your Lord.
He neither believed nor prayed; he denied, turned away, and strutted back to his family.
Woe to you, then woe! Again, woe to you, then woe!
Does man think he will be left aimless, with no commands and no return?
He was a drop, then a clot; Allah shaped him and made from him male and female.
Is the One who did this not able to bring the dead to life?

1.explain: Lā uqsimu: a strong oath; the lā adds force against the deniers’ claim. Allah swears by the Day of Resurrection itself. The unstated answer: you will surely be raised.

2.explain: An-nafs al-lawwāmah: the soul that blames itself, for sins and even for not doing more good. A believer keeps questioning his own motives; the sinner just carries on.

3.explain: Does man, the denier, think We won’t gather his bones after they rot and scatter? Bones are the frame of the whole body.
3.why: Reportedly ʿAdī ibn Rabīʿah asked the Prophet ﷺ when and how the Day would come, then said: “Even if I saw it, I would not believe you. Will Allah really gather bones?” Another report says it was about Abū Jahl.

4.explain: Balā: yes! Allah can reshape even his banān, the fingertips and their tiny bones, so the big ones are easy. Or: He could even fuse his fingers into one piece, like a hoof.

5.explain: Li-yafjura amāmah: he wants to keep sinning and put off repentance, or to deny what lies ahead of him. His problem isn’t a lack of proof.

6.explain: He asks ayyāna, “when?”, not to learn, but to mock and deny.

7.explain: Bariqa al-baṣar: eyes dazzled and staring, unable to blink or settle, at the terrors they used to deny.

8.explain: Khasafa al-qamar: the moon loses its light and goes dark.

9.explain: The sun and moon are brought together, either both losing their light and rolled up, or rising together from the west.

10.explain: Man cries, “Ayna al-mafarr? Where is the escape?”, looking for a way out of the horror.

11.explain: Kallā, lā wazar: no! No refuge, no fortress, no mountain to hide on.

12.explain: Al-mustaqarr: the final place of rest is with your Lord, where everyone stands to be judged. No one can hide or run.

13.explain: He is told what he qaddama wa akhkhara: every deed, first and last. Or: what he did in life, and practices he left behind that others followed, good or bad.

14.explain: Baṣīrah: he knows himself fully and is his own witness. His hearing, sight, hands and feet will testify.

15.explain: Maʿādhīrah: his excuses. Even if he pours out every one, none is accepted.

16.explain: Lā tuḥarrik bihi lisānak: don’t move your tongue with the Qurʾan to hurry, afraid a word will slip away. Wait until Jibrīl finishes.
16.why: The Prophet ﷺ found revelation hard and would move his lips quickly, repeating as Jibrīl recited, to memorize it. These ayat were revealed. Afterwards he listened in silence and recited once Jibrīl left, as Allah had promised.

17.explain: Jamʿahu wa qurʾānahu: it is on Us to gather it in your heart and to make you recite it. No need to fear forgetting.

18.explain: When We recite it to you through Jibrīl, follow its recitation: listen until he finishes, then recite it as he did.

19.explain: Bayānahu: explaining its meaning is also on Us. Allah guarantees both the words and the meaning.

20.explain: Kallā: no! The talk returns to the deniers: you love al-ʿājilah, this world that comes quickly, with its pleasures now.

21.explain: …and you leave the Hereafter, doing nothing for it, because its reward seems far off.

22.explain: Nāḍirah: faces fresh, bright and glowing with joy on that Day.

23.explain: Ilā rabbihā nāẓirah: looking at their Lord. The believers will see Allah with their own eyes, and nothing they are given is dearer to them than that.

24.explain: Bāsirah: other faces dark, gloomy and scowling.

25.explain: Sure that a fāqirah is about to hit them: a disaster so great it breaks the backbone (faqār).

26.explain: Kallā: when the soul rises to at-tarāqī, the collarbones at the base of the throat, at the moment of death.

27.explain: Man rāq: “Who can heal him?”, a doctor or someone to recite over him. Or it is the angels asking who will carry his soul up.

28.explain: The dying one is sure that al-firāq, the parting from this world, has come.

29.explain: Shin wraps against shin: his legs die and are bound in the shroud. Or: the last day of this world meets the first of the next, hardship on hardship.

30.explain: Al-masāq: on that Day he is driven to his Lord, to be repaid for his deeds.

31.explain: Fa-lā ṣaddaqa wa lā ṣallā: he did not believe and did not pray. Nothing good inside him, nothing good outside.
31.why: Reportedly revealed about Abū Jahl, who neither believed in the Prophet ﷺ nor prayed.

32.explain: Instead he denied the truth and turned away from faith and obedience, feeling completely safe.

33.explain: Yatamaṭṭā: then he went home to his family, stretching and strutting, pleased with himself, without a care.

34.explain: Awlā laka fa-awlā: woe to you, and woe! A threat, and a mockery of his swagger.
34.why: The Prophet ﷺ reportedly seized Abū Jahl’s clothes and said these words. Abū Jahl answered: “Are you threatening me? Neither you nor your Lord can do anything; I am the mightiest man in Makkah.” Reports differ on whether the ayah came before or after.

35.explain: Then woe to you, and woe! Four woes: either one for each of his failings, or at death, in the grave, at the Resurrection and in Hell.

36.explain: Sudā: left aimless, like camels grazing with no herder: no commands in this life, and no raising after death.

37.explain: Was he not a nuṭfah, a drop of fluid poured into the womb?

38.explain: Then he became an ʿalaqah, a clinging clot. Allah created him from it and proportioned him, perfecting his limbs.

39.explain: From it Allah made the two kinds, male and female.

40.explain: Is the One who did all this not able to bring the dead to life? Yes. Whoever recites this is taught to reply “Balā”, or “Subḥānaka, balā”: Glory be to You, yes.
